lanes.label: Elsewhere in scripture
lanes.range: Topics in other books wired to this one

nodes.d: The burden Habakkuk saw: his complaints about violence in Judah and the LORD's answers, the vision to wait for in which the just live by faith, woes on the proud, and a prayer ending in rejoicing in the LORD.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how Habakkuk moves from complaint to rejoicing?
ev: Describe the pattern of complaint and answer in chapters 1-2
Say how the book ends (3:17-19)

nodes.t: How long? The LORD raises up the Chaldeans
nodes.d: Habakkuk cries to the LORD about violence and perverted justice, and the LORD answers that he is raising up the fierce Chaldeans to sweep through the land.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what Habakkuk complains about and how the LORD answers?
ev: State Habakkuk's complaint (1:2-4)
Describe the LORD's answer (1:5-11)

nodes.t: Why dost thou look on the treacherous?
nodes.d: Habakkuk affirms that the LORD is everlasting and holy and has ordained the Chaldeans for judgment, but asks how a God of purer eyes than to see evil can look on the treacherous while they net the nations.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} state Habakkuk's second question and what he says about the LORD's character before asking it?
ev: Say what Habakkuk affirms about the LORD (1:12-13)
Describe the question he asks (1:13) and the picture of the net (1:14-17)

nodes.t: The vision to wait for; the just live by faith
nodes.d: Habakkuk stands on his watch; the LORD tells him to write the vision, which will surely come though it tarries, and contrasts the proud, whose soul is not upright, with the just, who shall live by his faith.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain the contrast of Habakkuk 2:4 and say what the LORD tells Habakkuk to do with the vision?
ev: Say what Habakkuk does and what the LORD tells him to do (2:1-3)
Read 2:4 and state the contrast
Find where Paul cites it (Romans 1:17)

nodes.t: Woes on the plunderer and idolater
nodes.d: The LORD pronounces a series of woes on the one who increases what is not his, builds a town with blood, shames his neighbour and trusts speechless idols, and says the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD's glory while he is in his holy temple.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} name some of the woes of Habakkuk 2 and the hope of 2:14?
ev: List the woes by their beginning words (2:6, 2:9, 2:12, 2:15, 2:19)
Read 2:14 and 2:20

nodes.t: Habakkuk's prayer: the LORD marches forth
nodes.d: Habakkuk prays that the LORD in wrath remember mercy, then recalls the LORD coming in glory with the nations driven apart, the sea and mountains shaken, and the LORD going forth for the salvation of his people with his anointed.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe what Habakkuk asks in 3:2 and what he recalls about the LORD in this prayer?
ev: Read the request of 3:2
Describe the LORD's appearing (3:3-6, 3:10-11) and its purpose (3:13)

nodes.t: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD
nodes.d: Habakkuk trembles at what he has heard, yet resolves that though fig tree, vine, olive, field and flock fail he will rejoice in the God of his salvation, who is his strength.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} say what Habakkuk chooses to do in Habakkuk 3:17-18 even when everything fails?
ev: List what fails in 3:17
Read the response in 3:18-19

nodes.d: Acts continues Luke's account from the ascension of Jesus (1:9) to Paul preaching at Rome (28:31): the Holy Ghost at Pentecost, the church in Jerusalem, the witness spreading to Judaea, Samaria and the Gentiles, and Paul's journeys, arrest and voyage to Rome.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} outline how the gospel spreads in Acts from Jerusalem to Rome?
ev: Say how Acts 1:8 gives the shape of the book (Jerusalem, Judaea, Samaria, the uttermost part)
Name the major sections: Peter in Jerusalem, Stephen and Philip, Saul's conversion, Cornelius, Paul's journeys, Paul's arrest and Rome

nodes.t: Paul preaches in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch
nodes.d: Invited to speak after the reading of the law and prophets, Paul traces Israel's story from Egypt through the judges and David to Jesus, whom God raised from the dead. He declares forgiveness of sins and that by Jesus all who believe are justified from what the law of Moses could not justify.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} summarise Paul's sermon from Israel's history to forgiveness through Jesus?
ev: Outline the history Paul recounts to reach Jesus (13:17-23)
State what Paul says is preached through Jesus (13:38-39)

nodes.d: Paul's letter to the Romans, from the greeting and the gospel theme (1:1-17) to its closing greetings and doxology (16:27).
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain in a few sentences what Romans is about, using 1:16-17?
ev: State the letter's theme from 1:16-17
Describe the movement: sin (1-3), justification (3-5), life in Christ and the Spirit (6-8), Israel (9-11), Christian living (12-16)

nodes.t: The gospel is the power of God
nodes.d: Paul introduces himself and states the letter's theme: the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, and in it the righteousness of God is revealed.
ev: Recite or paraphrase 1:16-17
Say what Paul calls himself in 1:1

nodes.d: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were turning to another gospel, to defend justification by faith, the freedom of the sons of God and life by the Spirit (1:1-6:18).
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why Paul wrote to the Galatians and what he says the true gospel is?
ev: Say what problem prompted the letter (1:6-9)
Name the three parts: Paul's defence (1-2), justification by faith (3-4), living by the Spirit (5-6)

nodes.t: Abraham, faith and the blessing for the nations
nodes.d: Paul argues that Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness, so those of faith are Abraham's children, and that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how Galatians 3:6-9 connects Abraham's faith to the Gentiles?
ev: Quote what Paul says Abraham did (3:6)
Explain who are the children of Abraham (3:7)
Say what the scripture foresaw (3:8)
Explain how Christ redeemed us from the curse (3:13-14)

nodes.t: Warning against wilful sin; endure and live by faith
nodes.d: The writer warns that no sacrifice remains for wilful sin after receiving the truth, reminds readers of their earlier endurance, and urges patience, since the just shall live by faith and they are not of those who draw back.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the writer asks the readers to remember and do in 10:32-39?
ev: Describe the warning of 10:26-29
State what the just shall do (10:38)
Tell what the readers endured before (10:32-34)

nodes.d: The letter to the Hebrews presents Jesus as God's Son, greater than angels and Moses, our great high priest after Melchizedek who mediates a better covenant by one sacrifice, and calls readers to faith and endurance.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain in a few sentences what Hebrews teaches about Jesus and what the readers are told to do?
ev: Describe the main parts: the Son (1-2), Moses and rest (3-4), the high priest (4-7), the new covenant and sacrifice (8-10), faith (11), endurance and exhortations (12-13)
